Statement from ACL and EACL 2026 Organizers
November 29, 2025 | BY webmaster
On Nov 27, OpenReview was notified of a software bug that allowed unauthorized access to authors, reviewers, and area chairs. We are grateful to the OpenReview team for fixing the issue quickly.

What is computational linguistics?
Computational linguistics is the scientific study of language from a computational perspective. Computational linguists are interested in providing computational models of various kinds of linguistic phenomena. These models may be "knowledge-based" ("hand-crafted") or "data-driven" ("statistical" or "empirical"). Work in computational linguistics is in some cases motivated from a scientific perspective in that one is trying to provide a computational explanation for a particular linguistic or psycholinguistic phenomenon; and in other cases the motivation may be more purely technological in that one wants to provide a working component of a speech or natural language system. Indeed, the work of computational linguists is incorporated into many working systems today, including speech recognition systems, text-to-speech synthesizers, automated voice response systems, web search engines, text editors, language instruction materials, to name just a few.
Popular computational linguistics textbooks include:
Christopher Manning and Hinrich Schütze (1999) Foundations of Statistical Natural Language Processing , Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA. MIT Press.
Also see the book's supplemental materials website at Stanford.
Daniel Jurafsky and James Martin (2008) An Introduction to Natural Language Processing, Computational Linguistics, and Speech Recognition , Second Edition. Prentice Hall.

CFP: The 2nd Workshop on NLP for the Iranian language family
October 06, 2026 | BY rayyanm
Event Notification Type:
Call for Papers
Abbreviated Title:
SilkRoadNLP 2027
Location:
EACL 2027
Tuesday, 9 March 2027 to Sunday, 14 March 2027
Country:
Greece
Contact Email:
rayyan.merchant@gmail.com
City:
Athens
Contact:
info@silkroadnlp.org
Website:
https://www.silkroadnlp.org
Submission Deadline:
Tuesday, 15 December 2026
SilkRoadNLP 2027 provides a platform for advancing Natural Language Processing (NLP), computational linguistics, and AI for the Iranian linguistic family—a diverse group of languages spoken across Iran, Afghanistan, Central and South Asia, and the Caucasus, as well as diaspora communities worldwide. We welcome work that bridges computational methods with linguistic, social, and cultural perspectives.
Despite major advances in multilingual NLP and large language models, the languages of the Iranian linguistic group remain underrepresented in mainstream research. While Persian has received some attention, many languages and varieties of the Iranian language family such as Kurdish, Balochi, Gilaki, Mazandarani, Luri, Pashto, Ossetic, Talysh, Zazaki, and others, continue to have limited digital presence, computational resources, benchmarks, and system support. Many are minority or endangered languages at risk of further technological marginalization. Within Persian, Iranian Persian, Dari, and Tajik differ in orthography, phonology, lexicon, and sociolinguistic context, with Tajik also differing in script.
Building on the inaugural workshop at EACL 2026, SilkRoadNLP continues its mission as a dedicated ACL-affiliated venue for computational research on the Iranian language family. The workshop aims to:
- Highlight advances in NLP analysis, datasets, benchmarks, models, and language technologies.
- Increase the visibility of Iranian languages and varieties underrepresented in mainstream NLP and AI.
- Address linguistic, cultural, sociopragmatic, and representational challenges in computational research.
- Foster collaboration across computational linguistics, linguistics, digital humanities, language documentation, education, and AI governance.
- Build a sustained international research community and shared ecosystem of resources for Iranian-language NLP.
We welcome research on all languages of the Iranian linguistic family, including contemporary, historical, regional, minority, endangered, heritage, and diaspora varieties.
2027 Theme: From Representation to Sovereignty: AI for Iranian Languages
This year’s theme moves beyond asking whether Iranian languages are represented in NLP and AI to examine how they are represented, who participates in developing the technologies around them, who governs linguistic and cultural data, and how language communities can retain meaningful agency over AI systems.
We especially welcome work on community-centered NLP, culturally grounded evaluation, data and language sovereignty, participatory development, and responsible AI across the development lifecycle. The workshop also aims to lay the groundwork for a collaborative Sovereign AI agenda for the Iranian linguistic family.
The theme complements the workshop’s broad scope. Contributions across Iranian-language NLP are welcome, whether or not they directly address the annual theme.
Topics of Interest:
We invite submissions on any aspect of NLP, computational linguistics, or AI relevant to the Iranian linguistic family, including contemporary, historical, regional, minority, endangered, heritage, and diaspora varieties. Topics include, but are not limited to:
- Computational linguistic analysis of Iranian languages: morphology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics, and typology.
- Resource creation, including corpora, benchmarks, and lexicons; language documentation and annotation.
- Speech and multimodal processing, including automatic speech recognition, text-to-speech, and multimodal learning.
- OCR, digitization tools, and script technologies.
- Language modeling and LLM adaptation, fine-tuning, and evaluation across domains.
- NLP for historical and extinct Iranian languages, such as Pahlavi, Avestan, and Sogdian, including applications in digital humanities and cultural heritage.
- NLP for regional varieties, dialects, heritage languages, and minority and endangered languages.
- Machine translation, transliteration, and cross-script processing.
- Evaluation frameworks, benchmarks, and shared tasks.
- Educational applications and language learning tools.
- Culturally grounded and sociopragmatic evaluation of language technologies.
- Community-centered NLP, participatory development, and collaboration with language communities.
- Data and language sovereignty, community agency, and governance of linguistic and cultural resources.
- Ethical and responsible AI across the language technology development lifecycle.
- Downstream and applied NLP, including information extraction, sentiment analysis, misinformation detection, information retrieval, social media analytics, and health and legal applications.
Contributions need not directly address the annual theme; we welcome work across the full range of Iranian-language NLP.
Shared Task: Tajik Cyrillic <-> Perso-Arabic Transliteration:
SilkRoadNLP 2027 will introduce a shared task on transliteration between Tajik Cyrillic and Perso-Arabic scripts. Building on an existing aligned dataset and established evaluation metrics, the task will provide a common benchmark for comparing transliteration systems and establishing reproducible baselines and state-of-the-art performance.
​The shared task aims to advance tool development and standardization for cross-script processing within the Iranian language family.
​Task specifications, data release and participation dates, evaluation procedures, and system paper submission instructions are being finalized and will be announced on the workshop website.
Paper Submission Format:
We invite the following categories of submissions:
- Long papers: Up to 8 pages of content (excluding references). Long papers should present substantial, original, unpublished contributions, with appropriate evaluation and analysis.
- Short papers / demo papers: Up to 4 pages of content (excluding references). Short papers should present a focused contribution that can be adequately described within this length. Demo papers should describe a system or tool and its relevance to the workshop.
​
We welcome research, position papers, resource papers, system demonstrations, and work-in-progress contributions within these categories.
All papers submitted to the workshop must be fully anonymized for double-blind review.
​All submissions must use the official ACL style template and be submitted as PDF files. References, appendices, a dedicated Limitations section, and an optional Ethical Considerations section do not count toward the content page limit. Appendices should appear after the references. The main paper must contain the information necessary to assess the contribution; reviewers are not required to read supplementary materials.
Submission & Review
Direct submissions will be made through the workshop’s OpenReview submission page. We will also accept papers with completed ACL Rolling Review (ARR) reviews, including a meta-review. Instructions for submitting ARR-reviewed papers and the workshop submission link will be announced on our website.
​Camera-ready instructions will be provided with acceptance notifications. Accepted papers will be published in the ACL Anthology as part of the EACL 2027 workshop proceedings.
Hybrid Participation:
The workshop will be held in a collaborative hybrid format, combining in-person sessions in Athens with online participation to ensure wide accessibility. The workshop will feature live-streamed talks, virtual poster sessions, and interactive Q&A opportunities for remote attendees. Final details on the hybrid setup will be shared closer to the event in coordination with EACL 2027.
Important Dates:
- Call for Papers: October 8, 2026
- Direct Submission Deadline: December 15, 2026
- Pre-reviewed ARR Commitment Deadline: December 22, 2026
- Notification of Acceptance: January 5, 2027
- Camera-ready Papers Due: January 9, 2027
- Poster Boards and presentation slides Due: February 5, 2027
- Workshop Date: TBA / March 9-14, 2027
​All deadlines are 11:59 PM UTC-12 (“anywhere on Earth”).
Diversity & Inclusion
SilkRoadNLP is committed to inclusive participation. We strongly encourage submissions from early-career researchers, independent scholars, and institutions in low-resource regions. The workshop will support hybrid participation (onsite + virtual) to maximize accessibility.
Feel free to contact us with any questions.

Call for Nominations of ARR co-Editors-in-Chief
October 05, 2026 | BY Sarvnaz Karimi
Event Notification Type:
Other
Abbreviated Title:
Location:
State:
Country:
Contact Email:
sarvnaz.karimi@monash.edu
xiaodan.zhu@queensu.ca
City:
Contact:
Sarvnaz Karimi
Xiaodan Zhu
Website:
Submission Deadline:
Sunday, 15 November 2026
Call for Nominations of ARR co-Editors-in-Chief
The ACL Rolling Review (ARR) initiative is seeking nominations
(including self-nominations) for co-Editors-in-Chief (henceforth
“EiCs”, with the “co-” understood) positions, serving a 2.5-3-year
term*. Successful candidates should be able to start in
January/February 2027 or as early as possible.
ARR is increasingly used as the main submission channel for *CL
conferences. In the recent two cycles for ACL and EMNLP, ARR has
received over 10,000 and 17,000 submissions in each cycle,
respectively. To continue supporting these large cycles and to keep
improving the ARR reviewing process, especially with the recently
announced ARR sustainable reviewing policy, there is a pressing need
to scale the EiCs team managing the 10-week cycles. EiCs rotate to
lead reviewing cycles. However, the entire team coordinates and
oversees the following activities:
Recruit and manage (senior) area chairs ((S)ACs) and reviewers
Coordinate with conference program chairs, becoming guest PCs during
cycles tied to *CL conferences
Oversee review forms and CFPs
Review and update submission tracks
Make final desk reject decisions (in collaboration with PCs in
conference-associated cycles)
Provide reports to the ACL Exec
General work on the ARR system hosted on OpenReview
Coordinate with the rest of the ARR team, including support,
communications, etc.
Participate in review policy development in coordination with ACL peer
review committee, Publication Ethics Committee and other ACL bodies
The ideal candidate would have a strong publication record across more
than one NLP research area and a solid record as an outstanding member
of the *CL community. Experience serving in ARR as SAC and/or AC is
highly valued, as is having served as a past PC in one of our top *CL
conferences and/or as an EiC for one of our *CL journals. At a
minimum, candidates should have at least some experience in managing
submission and reviewing processes, for example, as workshop
co-organizers.
Being an ARR Editor-in-Chief is a major, ongoing time commitment
requiring, on average, ~5-10 hours a week in off-duty cycles, and
approximately ~25-30 hours a week in on-duty cycles. It can absorb a
significant amount of time during peak cycle phases. That is, when an
EiC is co-leading a cycle, it is expected that they can dedicate a
large portion of their time during these peak critical times. However,
contributing to our community this way is also a very rewarding
experience. We are aware that the ARR process needs to continue to
improve; we are looking for candidates with ideas on improving what we
do who are also eager to dedicate their energy and time to help us
implement better reviewing practices and workflows.
ARR is a diverse team, and we are determined to keep it that way. This
includes recruiting EiCs from different continents and backgrounds.
Due to the requirements we specified, senior members of the ACL
community are considered.
Nomination procedure
Nominations should be submitted via email to EiC member Sarvnaz Karimi
( sarvnaz.karimi [at] gmail.com ), with a CC to EiC member Xiaodan Zhu
( xiaodan.zhu [at] queensu.ca ), by November 15th, 2026, subject line
“Nomination for ARR co-EiC”, and should contain the following
information:
Name, email address, and website of the nominee
If not a self-nomination, confirmation that the nominee is willing to
serve (a dated excerpt of an email from the nominee suffices); if a
self-nomination, a statement affirming willingness to serve.
Statement of nominee’s goals/vision for ARR and/or relevant prior
experience and/or reasons for interest in the position. The length of
the statement is up to the nominator, but 1 paragraph may suffice, and
more than 4 paragraphs are not anticipated to be necessary.
Nominations will be acknowledged by reply email; should acknowledgment
not be received within 3 days, please resend your email.
The existing ARR EiC team will evaluate the nominations and make
decisions, after which the search committee chair will contact the
selected nominee via email.
* The last 6 months are not considered as full on EiCs but more of a
transition period to support training of new EiCs.

ACL 2027 Call for Papers
ACL 2027 invites the submission of long and short papers featuring substantial, original, and unpublished research in all aspects of Computational Linguistics and Natural Language Processing. ACL 2027 has a goal of a diverse technical program—in addition to traditional research results, papers may contribute negative findings, survey an area, announce the creation of a new resource, argue a position, report novel linguistic insights derived using existing computational techniques, and reproduce, or fail to reproduce, previous results. As in recent years, some of the presentations at the conference will feature papers accepted by the Transactions of the ACL (TACL) and the Computational Linguistics (CL) journals. We also introduce the Special Theme Homogenization and knowledge collapse in LLMs, which we hope will stimulate exciting research contributions.
Papers submitted to ACL 2027, but not selected for the main conference, will also automatically be considered for publication in the Findings of the Association of Computational Linguistics.

Paper Submission Information
Dual submissions are not allowed! Please check the ARR Call for Papers for details. Papers must be submitted, at latest, by the ARR 202 7 January cycle. Papers that have received reviews and a meta-review from ARR (whether from the ARR 2027 January cycle or an earlier ARR cycle) may be committed to ACL via the commitment link (not available yet). ACL has adopted a sustainable reviewing policy starting from October 2026. Read the full announcement .
Submission Topics
ACL 2027 aims to have a broad technical program of papers that make a contribution to computational processing of natural language. Relevant topics for the conference include, but are not limited to, the following areas (see also the ARR submission scope ):
Special Theme: Homogenization and knowledge collapse in LLMs
Clinical and Biomedical Applications
Computational Social Science and Cultural Analytics
Dialogue and Interactive Systems
Discourse and Pragmatics
Efficient Methods for NLP
Ethics, Bias, and Fairness
Human-Centered NLP and Human-AI Interaction
Information Extraction
Information Retrieval and Text Mining
Interpretability and Analysis of Models for NLP
Language Diversity and NLP for Low-resourced Languages
Language Modeling
LLM Agents for NLP
Linguistic Theories, Cognitive Modeling, and Psycholinguistics
Machine Learning for NLP
Machine Translation
Multilingualism and Cross-Lingual NLP
Multimodality and Language Grounding to Vision, Robotics and Beyond
NLP and Code Models
NLP and Symbolic Reasoning
NLP Applications
Phonology, Morphology, and Word Segmentation
Question Answering
Semantics: Lexical and Sentence-Level
Sentiment Analysis, Stylistic Analysis, and Argument Mining
Speech Recognition, Text-to-Speech and Spoken Language Understanding
Summarization
Syntax: Tagging, Chunking and Parsing
ACL 2027 Theme Track: Homogenization and knowledge collapse in LLMs
Recent research suggests that, despite their impressive capabilities and broad applicability, LLMs tend to collapse diversity in their outputs. As LLMs become fundamental tools for information retrieval and creative expression, this raises concerns about a shift from rich, human-driven discourse toward what has been called a “generative monoculture” where current training and alignment practices may inadvertently compress the wide spectrum of human thought into a limited range of stereotyped outputs. This special theme invites papers investigating whether LLMs produce low-diversity responses, rely on repetitive linguistic structures, and converge on a narrow set of solutions, potentially acting as drivers of cultural homogenization.
The theme track invites empirical and theoretical work as well as surveys and position papers reflecting on Homogenization and knowledge collapse in LLMs from different perspectives. Possible topics of research include (but are not limited to) the following:
Metrics and methodologies for assessing homogenization, cultural flattening and knowledge collapse trends in LLMs.
Identification of the mechanisms that could be inducing these trends, e.g. analyses of training data, alignment strategies, decoding methods, and optimization objectives that may contribute to reduced output diversity, along with proposals for mitigation.
Search space exploration vs. convergence in generative models: To what extent do LLMs explore the breadth of possible responses versus converging on high-probability, stereotyped outputs? What are the trade-offs between coherence, safety, and diversity?
Human vs. Model Diversity: interdisciplinary perspectives on epistemic diversity and Knowledge Representation in LLMs, including comparative studies of variability in human- vs. LLM-generated responses across domains (e.g., linguistic, cultural, cognitive), drawing on insights from linguistics, cognitive science, sociology, and related fields.
Cross-linguistic homogenization: When queried in different languages, do LLMs respond more uniformly than humans would? To what extent are LLMs capable of adapting their responses to the writing and cultural norms that best associate to the query language? Do LLMs produce more uniform text in lower-resource languages?
LLMs and ideological polarization: Under what conditions might LLMs contribute to homogenized or fragmented discourse? This includes investigation on whether and how LLMs compress, filter, or privilege certain forms of knowledge, and the implications for pluralism in knowledge systems.
Theme track submissions can be either long or short. We anticipate having a special session for this theme at the conference and a Thematic Paper Award in addition to other categories of awards.
Two Stage Review: Submission to ARR, Commitment to ACL
ACL 2027 will use ACL Rolling Review (ARR) as a reviewing system, but final decisions will be made by the conference. Both submissions of articles for review and commitment of reviewed articles to the conference will be performed via the Open Review platform. Specifically, authors will follow a two-step process:
Authors submit articles to ARR , where submissions receive reviews and meta-reviews from ARR reviewers and action editors;
Authors commit their reviewed articles to a publication venue (e.g., ACL 2027), where Senior Area Chairs and Program Chairs make acceptance decisions from the ARR reviews and meta-reviews.
Authorship during commitment. During the commitment phase, it is not allowed to modify the author list (i.e., addition/deletion of authors is not allowed).
ACL 2027 has chosen this approach in coordination with *CL 2027 conferences, which are adopting the same procedure and a coordinated submission plan to allow maximum flexibility during their submission periods for the authors. At each cycle, after a paper has been fully reviewed, authors have the option to commit their paper to a conference, or revise and resubmit for another round of reviews.
The reviewing process will continue to be double-blind. Reviewers will not see authors, nor will authors see reviewers and reviews on ARR will not be made publicly visible. However, authors will be given the option through ARR to make their anonymized submitted articles publicly visible.
Paper Submission Details
Both long and short paper submissions should follow all of the ARR submission requirements , including:
Long Papers (8 pages) and Short Papers (4 pages)
Instructions for Two-Way Anonymized Review
Authorship
Citation and Comparison
Multiple Submission Policy , Resubmission Policy , and Withdrawal Policy
ACL’s Publication Ethics Policy , and ARR’s Ethics Policy including the responsible NLP research checklist
ACL’s Disclosure Policy
Limitations
Writing Assistance
Paper Submission and Templates
Optional Supplementary Materials
Final versions of accepted papers will be given one additional page of content (up to 9 pages for long papers, up to 5 pages for short papers) to address reviewers’ comments.
Presentation at the Conference
All accepted papers must be presented at the conference to appear in the proceedings. The conference will include both in-person and virtual presentation options. Papers without at least one presenting author registered by the early registration deadline may be subject to rejection. Long and short papers will be presented orally or as posters, as determined by the program committee. While short papers will be distinguished from long papers in the proceedings, there will be no distinction in the proceedings between papers presented orally and papers presented as posters.
Contact Information

Yusuke Miyao, The University of Tokyo

===== http://www.aclweb.org/aclwiki/Resources_by_paper =====
Resources by paper - ACL Wiki
Resources by paper
From ACL Wiki
Jump to navigation
Jump to search
The purpose of this section of the ACL wiki is to connect papers to their resources, such as datasets, software, corpora, demos, slides, and videos.
Papers are organized by venue (conference, workshop, journal) and year. For each venue and year, there is a list of papers (titles and authors) with hypertext links to the PDF file for each paper and hypertext links to any resources used or introduced by the paper. If it becomes necessary to move a PDF file or a resource to another website, the entry for the paper can easily be updated with the latest locations.
Please contribute! Benefits include:
visibility for your work
reproducible research
future collaborations
faster-paced innovation
links can be updated as resources move or grow
